# GitHub discovery and topics

Use this guide when configuring the GitHub About panel, topics, README, or social preview. Check edition-specific docs if the target is GitHub Enterprise Server.

## Metadata and discovery

- Choose a recognizable repository name. Put the project category and primary outcome naturally in the About description and README lead. Add a canonical website, docs or demo URL if maintained. Highlight the project’s primary release or package channel, and enable only features the maintainers operate. [GitHub Quickstart for repositories](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/creating-and-managing-repositories/quickstart-for-repositories)
- GitHub repository search supports qualifiers such as in:name, in:description, in:readme, topic:, language:, and org:. Test a few queries a real user would use. Distinguish repository search from code and web search. New or changed metadata may take time to be indexed. Report discoverability checks as observations. [Searching for repositories](https://docs.github.com/en/search-github/searching-on-github/searching-for-repositories)
- Use the first screen to show what the project solves, key supported platforms or users, and one quick start. Keep badges tied to current checks, releases, supported package registries, or compatibility. Link to canonical documentation, record prerequisites and platform differences, and move long reference tables or niche instructions lower down. Use descriptive link text and alt text, clear headings, fenced examples, relative paths for repo content, and selective details elements. Test GitHub’s rendered view at a narrow width. [README behavior](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-readmes), [GitHub Markdown syntax](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/getting-started-with-writing-and-formatting-on-github/basic-writing-and-formatting-syntax), [Collapsed sections](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/writing-on-github/working-with-advanced-formatting/organizing-information-with-collapsed-sections)
- Set a readable social preview when public sharing matters. GitHub recommends 1280 × 640 pixels, with a 640 × 320 minimum and a file under 1 MB. Check the rendered crop and avoid tiny text. Verify About links and the public README without relying on editor or contributor permissions. [Social media preview](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/customizing-your-repositorys-social-media-preview)

## Topic selection

1. **Always baseline the languages.** Inventory the maintained languages used to build, run, or operate the project. Cross-check the Languages panel or GitHub languages API against source, manifests, and build entry points. Use canonical community slugs such as typescript, python, or shell. Include a small maintained implementation language when it matters to users. Exclude generated code, vendored code, bundled assets, fixtures, and incidental format files, unless the language or format is itself a supported deliverable. For a docs-only repo, use an appropriate actual format or ecosystem topic when meaningful and avoid inventing a runtime language. Investigate discrepancies before changing Linguist attributes. [About repository languages](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-repository-languages), [Linguist overrides](https://github.com/github-linguist/linguist/blob/main/docs/overrides.md)
2. **Add only topics with a reason.** Consider the primary purpose, artifact type, maintained integrations, and specific ecosystem or platform. Compare existing topic pages for names and audience fit. Require a concrete source file, release, or user-facing feature that justifies each topic. Remove synonyms, irrelevant trending topics, incidental dependencies, and stale claims. Start small and stop when a new topic adds little information.
3. **Check the platform rules.** GitHub allows up to 20 topics, each at most 50 characters, using lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens. Topic names are public even when created on private repositories. Treat 20 as a cap. If meaningful candidates exceed it, preserve core language coverage first, then prioritize the intended audience’s most precise terms. If the languages alone exceed the cap, record the omitted languages and keep the full inventory in documentation. [Classifying repositories with topics](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/classifying-your-repository-with-topics)
4. **Review and verify.** Fetch existing state first. Preserve user-selected topics that still apply, and only remove unrelated topics when editing is in scope. Use the About panel, gh repo edit with topic additions and explicit removals, or the REST API with the complete intended set. The REST replacement endpoint overwrites the prior set. Read back topics and check the repository UI. Reassess when runtime languages or supported integrations change. [GitHub CLI repo edit](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_repo_edit), [Repository REST API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/repos)

For a read-only CLI inventory, substitute the actual repository coordinates.

~~~sh
gh repo view OWNER/REPO --json description,homepageUrl,repositoryTopics,defaultBranchRef,visibility
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/languages
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/topics --jq '.names'
~~~
